questions.title: What a header is
questions.text: What is a **header** in a word-processed document?

options.content: The title of a section in the body text
An area in the top margin whose content is repeated on every page
A note at the bottom of a page linked to a number in the text
The first row of a table

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: A is a heading, C a footnote, D a table's header row.

questions.title: Header vs heading
questions.text: A header and a heading are the same thing.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: A heading is a title inside the body text; a header is the repeated area in the top margin of every page.

questions.title: Items for headers and footers
questions.text: Select **two** items that are suitable for the header or footer of a project's technical documentation.

options.content: Page number
A screenshot of the login screen
Document title and version number
The full data dictionary

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Page numbers as fields
questions.text: Why should page numbers be inserted as a **page-number field** in the footer rather than typed on each page?

options.content: Fields print in colour
The numbers update automatically when pages are added or removed
Fields make the document file smaller
Typed numbers cannot appear in a footer

scheme.mark_scheme: B

questions.title: Version number in the header
questions.text: Three developers edit the design document of a project. Why should the **version number and date** be in its header?

options.content: So every printed page shows which copy it is, and readers can check they have the latest version
So the word processor can save the file automatically
So the table of contents can be created
So the document cannot be copied

scheme.mark_scheme: A

questions.title: Header options
questions.text: Match each header/footer option to its use.

right.text: No header on the title page
Page numbers on the outside edge of a printed booklet
Each chapter shows its own title in the header

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R1, L2–R2, L3–R3. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: What a footnote is
questions.text: Which statement describes a **footnote**?

options.content: Text repeated at the bottom margin of every page
A note at the bottom of the same page, linked to a reference mark in the text
A list of all notes at the end of the document
The last paragraph of a chapter

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: A describes a footer, C describes endnotes.

questions.title: Inserting a footnote
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

In Microsoft Word a footnote is inserted from the [[1]] tab. The small number in the main text that links to the footnote is called the reference [[2]].

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) References (2) mark

questions.title: Footnote or endnote
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row.

prefill: Appears at the bottom of the same page as its reference
All notes are collected at the end of the document
The reader can see the note without turning pages

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 Footnote (1); 2 Endnote (1); 3 Footnote (1)

questions.title: Uses of footnotes
questions.text: Select the **three** good uses of footnotes in project documentation.

options.content: Giving the source of a fact or quotation
Explaining a technical term such as SQL
Giving the main installation instructions
Adding a small extra detail, e.g. the server's specification
Showing the page number
Showing the document title on every page

scheme.mark_scheme: A and B and D. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Main instructions belong in the body text; page numbers and titles belong in the footer/header.

questions.title: Where does it go?
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show the best place for each item in a project report.

prefill: The website a statistic in the text was taken from

scheme.mark_scheme: Project title and version number – Header (1); "Confidential" notice and "Page 4 of 30" – Footer (1); The website a statistic in the text was taken from – Footnote (1); The heading "3. Testing" – Body text (1)

points.criterion: Row 1: Project title and version number
Row 3: The website a statistic in the text was taken from

scheme.model_answer: Project title and version number: Header; "Confidential" notice and "Page 4 of 30": Footer; The website a statistic in the text was taken from: Footnote; The heading "3. Testing": Body text.

questions.title: Test plan column
questions.text: A test-plan table has the columns *Test no.*, *Test data*, *Type of data* and *Expected result*. Name the column that is filled in **after** the test is run and compared with the expected result.

scheme.mark_scheme: Actual result

questions.title: Table features
questions.text: Match each table feature to its purpose.

right.text: Shows the heading of each column
Gives the table a number and title, e.g. Table 3. Test plan
Makes one cell span several columns
Shows the column headings again on each new page

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R1, L2–R2, L3–R3, L4–R4. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Tables in project documents
questions.text: Match each table to the columns it would contain.

right.text: Task, start date, end date, person responsible
Test no., test data, type of data, expected result, actual result
Field name, data type, size, validation, description

scheme.mark_scheme: Test plan – Test no., test data, type of data, expected result, actual result; Data dictionary – Field name, data type, size, validation, description; Project schedule – Task, start date, end date, person responsible; Troubleshooting table – Error message, cause, solution. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Good practice for tables
questions.text: Select the **three** examples of good practice when formatting a table in a project document.

options.content: A header row with clear, bold column headings
A numbered caption such as "Table 3. Test plan"
Several kinds of data mixed in one column
Repeating the header row when the table continues on the next page
Using a different colour for every cell
Leaving out column headings to save space

scheme.mark_scheme: A and B and D. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: What a table of contents is
questions.text: What is a **table of contents**?

options.content: A table of the test results
A list of the document's headings with their page numbers, at the start of the document
A list of the sources used in the footnotes
The header of the first page

scheme.mark_scheme: B

questions.title: Updating the TOC
questions.text: After pages are added to a document, an automatic table of contents should be updated (Update Table) so that its page numbers are correct.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.

questions.title: A heading is missing from the TOC
questions.text: Daniyar inserted an automatic table of contents, but the heading *"2.2 Data dictionary"* does not appear in it. What is the most likely reason?

options.content: The heading was made bold and large by hand instead of using a heading style
The heading is too long
The document has no footer
The heading contains a number

scheme.mark_scheme: A
scheme.explanation: An automatic TOC is built only from text formatted with heading styles (Heading 1, Heading 2…).

questions.title: Creating a TOC
questions.text:
Complete the method.

Format every chapter title with the [[1]] 1 style. Insert the table of contents from the [[2]] tab in Microsoft Word. After editing the document, click Update [[3]] so the page numbers are correct.

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) heading (2) references / reference (3) table / table of contents / field

questions.title: Technical documentation or user guide?
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show where each item belongs.

prefill: Data dictionary of the database tables
How to install the program, step by step
Error messages and how to solve them

scheme.mark_scheme: Data dictionary of the database tables – Technical documentation (1); How to install the program, step by step – User guide (1); Algorithms and annotated code listings – Technical documentation (1); Error messages and how to solve them – User guide (1)

points.criterion: Row 1: Data dictionary of the database tables
Row 2: How to install the program, step by step
Row 3: Algorithms and annotated code listings
Row 4: Error messages and how to solve them

scheme.model_answer: Data dictionary of the database tables: Technical documentation; How to install the program, step by step: User guide; Algorithms and annotated code listings: Technical documentation; Error messages and how to solve them: User guide.

questions.title: Headers and footers in a technical document
questions.text: Three students are writing the 40-page **technical documentation** for *Sabaq*, a timetable app for their school. Each of them edits the document and prints pages to show the teacher.

parts.title: Header and footer contents
parts.text: State **two** suitable items for the **header** and **two** suitable items for the **footer** of this document.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Header, any two (1 each): document / project title (Sabaq); section / chapter name; version number; date; school name / logo
Footer, any two (1 each): page number / Page X of Y; author(s); copyright / confidentiality notice; file name; date / version
The same item may not be credited twice.
scheme.model_answer: Header: Sabaq — Technical documentation; version 2.0, 12.11.2026. Footer: Page 7 of 40; authors' names.

parts.title: Page-number field
parts.text: Explain why the page numbers should be inserted as a **field** rather than typed on each page.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- a field is updated automatically / the numbers change by themselves (1)
- when pages are added, removed or moved during editing, so the numbers stay correct with no retyping / match the table of contents (1)

points.criterion: Stays correct when pages change / saves retyping

scheme.model_answer: A page-number field updates automatically, so when the students add or remove pages the numbers stay correct without anyone retyping them.

parts.title: Version in the header
parts.text: Explain why the **version number and date** should appear in the header of this document.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- three students edit and print the document, so there are several copies (1)
- every page shows which version it belongs to, so readers can check they have the latest copy / do not work from an old one (1)

points.criterion: Identify the latest version on every page

scheme.model_answer: Because three people edit and print the document, the version and date on every page show which copy a page belongs to, so nobody works from or hands in an out-of-date version.

parts.title: Header and heading
parts.text: Describe the difference between a **header** and a **heading**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- header: in the top margin, repeated automatically on every page (1)
- heading: a title in the body text above one section, appears once (1)

points.criterion: Heading: in the body text, once

scheme.model_answer: A header is in the top margin and is repeated on every page; a heading is a title inside the body text that introduces one section and appears only once.

questions.title: Footnotes in a project report
questions.text:
Madina's project report contains this sentence:

*"About 70% of pupils use the canteen every day, so the new ordering system must handle 600 orders between 12:00 and 12:40 using the school's server."*

The percentage comes from a school survey and the server's specification is not explained anywhere in the report.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- a note at the bottom of the same page (1)
- linked to a (numbered) reference mark in the text / gives a source or explanation (1)

points.criterion: Linked to a reference mark / source or explanation

scheme.model_answer: A footnote is a note at the bottom of the same page, linked by a small reference number in the text, that gives a source or extra explanation.

parts.title: Footnotes in this sentence
parts.text: Identify **two** footnotes Madina should add to this sentence. Say what each footnote would contain.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- a footnote after "70%" giving the source: the school survey, date / who carried it out (1)
- a footnote after "server" giving the server's specification / explaining the technical detail (1)
scheme.model_answer: 1: after "70%" — Source: school canteen survey, October 2026. 2: after "server" — Windows Server 2022, 16 GB RAM.

parts.title: Footnotes or endnotes
parts.text: Explain **one** advantage of using footnotes rather than endnotes in this report.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the note is on the same page as the text it explains (1)
- so the reader does not have to turn to the end of the document / can check the source immediately (1)

points.criterion: No need to turn to the end / immediate

scheme.model_answer: Footnotes are on the same page as the sentence, so the reader can check the survey source immediately without turning to the end of the report.

parts.title: Automatic footnotes
parts.text: Explain why Madina should insert footnotes with the word processor's **Insert Footnote** tool instead of typing small numbers and notes herself.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the tool numbers footnotes automatically / renumbers them when notes are added, deleted or moved (1)
- and keeps each note on the same page as its reference mark when the text moves (1)

points.criterion: Note stays on the same page as its mark

scheme.model_answer: The tool numbers the footnotes automatically and renumbers them if she adds one earlier, and it keeps each note at the bottom of the page where its reference mark is, even when the text moves.

questions.title: Test plan table
questions.text: The *Smart Canteen* login form accepts passwords that are **8 to 20 characters** long. The test results are recorded in a table in the testing section of the documentation.

parts.title: Type of test data
parts.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show the type of each item of test data for the password length rule (8 to 20 characters).

scheme.mark_scheme: Kazakh2026!  (11 characters) – Normal (1); abc  (3 characters) – Erroneous (1); Abcdefg1  (8 characters) – Boundary (1); a password of 25 characters – Erroneous (1)
scheme.model_answer: Kazakh2026!  (11 characters): Normal; abc  (3 characters): Erroneous; Abcdefg1  (8 characters): Boundary; a password of 25 characters: Erroneous.

parts.title: Column headings
parts.text: State **two** column headings, other than *Test data* and *Type of data*, that the test-plan table should have.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): test number; description / purpose of the test; expected result / outcome; actual result / outcome; pass / fail; comment / action taken

parts.title: Why a table
parts.text: Explain **two** reasons why the test results should be presented in a table rather than in paragraphs of text.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Two reasons, each 1 mark for the point + 1 for the explanation:
- each item is in its own row / column (1) so expected and actual results are easy to compare / failed tests found quickly (1)
- information is easy to scan / find by row and column (1) so the reader / teacher can check a test quickly (1)
- empty cells show missing results (1) so no test is forgotten (1)
- consistent structure for every test (1) so the same details are recorded each time / easy to add tests (1)
scheme.model_answer: Each test has its own row with separate columns, so the expected and actual results sit side by side and failed tests are found at once. The table also has the same columns for every test, so empty cells show straight away if a result is missing.

questions.title: Table of contents
questions.text: Daniyar's 35-page project report has five chapters (Analysis, Design, Development, Testing, Evaluation), each with several sections. He typed the table of contents by hand.

parts.title: Create an automatic TOC
parts.text: Describe how Daniyar should create an **automatic** table of contents.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- apply heading styles: Heading 1 to chapter titles, Heading 2 to section titles (1)
- insert the table of contents (References → Table of Contents) at the start, after the title page (1)
- update the table (Update Table) after editing so the headings and page numbers are correct (1)
scheme.model_answer: He formats chapter titles with Heading 1 and section titles with Heading 2, inserts a table of contents from References → Table of Contents on page 2, and clicks Update Table after every change.

parts.title: Automatic vs typed
parts.text: Explain **one** advantage of an automatic table of contents over one typed by hand.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- page numbers / headings are updated automatically when pages move (1)
- so the TOC stays accurate with no retyping / fewer errors / entries are links to the sections (1)
scheme.model_answer: When chapters move, Update Table corrects every page number automatically, so the contents stay accurate without retyping.

parts.title: TOC and footer
parts.text: Explain how the table of contents and the **page numbers in the footer** work together to help the reader.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the TOC gives the page number of each section (1)
- the footer shows the number of the current page, so the reader can find / turn to that page quickly (1)

points.criterion: TOC gives page of each section
Footer shows current page to find it

scheme.model_answer: The table of contents tells the reader that, for example, Testing starts on page 21, and the page number in the footer shows which page they are on, so they can turn straight to it.

questions.title: User guide
questions.text: The developers of *Sabaq* also write a **user guide** for teachers who will use the app.

parts.title: Contents of a user guide
parts.text: State **two** items that should be included in the user guide.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): installation instructions; hardware / software requirements; how to carry out each task, step by step; screenshots; error messages and solutions / troubleshooting; FAQ; backup procedures; contact / help details
scheme.model_answer: Installation instructions; a troubleshooting table of error messages and solutions.

parts.title: Features that help teachers
parts.text: Explain how **headers and footers**, **footnotes** and a **table of contents** each make the user guide easier for teachers to use.

scheme.mark_scheme:
One mark for each feature linked to the user:
- headers / footers: title and page numbers on every page, so teachers know where they are / find pages from the TOC (1)
- footnotes: explain technical terms / give extra detail without cluttering the instructions (1)
- table of contents: teachers find the section for a task quickly (1)
scheme.model_answer: The footer's page numbers and the header's title show teachers where they are in the guide; footnotes explain technical words without making the steps harder to read; the table of contents lets them go straight to the task they need.

summary: Using headers and footers, footnotes, tables and a table of contents when documenting a software project — what each is for, what it should contain, how to insert it in a word processor, and good practice for technical and user documentation.

blocks.content: Every software project produces **documentation**: the **requirements specification**, the **design** (DFDs, ERD, data dictionary), the **test plan and results**, **technical documentation** for developers and a **user guide** for the people who will use the system. Good documents are **consistent, easy to navigate and easy to check**. Four word-processing features help with this: **headers and footers**, **footnotes**, **tables** and a **table of contents**.

The written documents produced during the system life cycle that **describe the system** — how it was analysed, designed, built and tested (**technical documentation**) and how to install and use it (**user documentation**).

blocks.caption: The parts of a document page

blocks.title: Technical documentation vs user guide
rows: Algorithms, code listings, data dictionary, ERD, DFD, test plan, hardware/software requirements
Installation instructions, how to carry out tasks, screenshots, error messages and solutions, FAQ, backup procedures
To **maintain and improve** the system later

items.title: Header and footer
items.content: Text repeated in the top and bottom margins of every page — title, version, page number.

items.title: Footnote
items.content: A numbered note at the bottom of the page — a source or explanation.

items.title: Table
items.content: Rows and columns of cells — test plans, data dictionaries, schedules.

items.title: Table of contents
items.content: A list of headings with page numbers, built automatically from heading styles.

blocks.content: A **header** is an area in the **top margin** of every page, and a **footer** an area in the **bottom margin**, whose content is **automatically repeated on every page** (or every page of a section) of the document.
A placeholder in a document that the word processor **fills in and updates automatically**, e.g. the **page number**, total number of pages, date or file name.

blocks.caption: A header and footer are typed once and repeated on every page

blocks.title: What headers and footers usually contain
rows: The reader always knows which document a page belongs to
Helps the reader find their place
Shows whether the copy is up to date — vital for project documents that change
Navigation; matches the table of contents; shows if pages are missing
Who to contact about the document
Where the electronic file is stored

items.title: Advantages
items.content:
- Entered **once** and appear on **every page** automatically — saves time.
- **Consistent** layout across the whole document.
- **Fields** (page number, date, number of pages) update **automatically** when pages are added or removed.
- Keep important information (title, version) visible when pages are **printed or separated**.

items.title: Options in a word processor
items.content:
- **Different first page** — no header on the title page.
- **Different odd and even pages** — e.g. page numbers on the outside edge for a printed booklet.
- **Sections** — each chapter can have its own header text (e.g. the chapter title).
- Insert **fields**: page number, total pages, date, file name.

blocks.title: Header vs heading
rows: In the **top margin**, outside the body text
**In the body text**, above a section
The title of one section, e.g. "3. Testing"
Used for the table of contents?

blocks.title: Inserting a header and footer (Microsoft Word / Google Docs)
items: **Insert → Header** (or double-click in the top margin) and type the document title and version.
**Insert → Footer**, then **Insert → Page number** (choose a format such as "Page X of Y").
Tick **Different first page** if the title page should have no header.
Close the header/footer area (double-click in the body text or press Esc).

blocks.title: Worked example — headers and footers for a canteen project
blocks.content:
Aruzhan is writing the design document for the **Smart Canteen** project at NIS Aktobe.
- **Header:** "Smart Canteen — Design document · v1.3 · 12.11.2026" — readers can see at once that a printed page belongs to the newest version.
- **Footer:** "Page 5 of 18" inserted as **fields** on the left, "Author: A. Nurlanovna" on the right.
- **Different first page:** the title page has no header or footer.
- When she adds a new section, all page numbers and "of 18" change automatically — she never types a page number by hand.

- Typing the page number by hand on each page instead of inserting a **page-number field**.
- Confusing a **header** (top margin, repeated) with a **heading** (a title in the body text).
- Forgetting the **version number** — two people then work from different copies.

A **note at the bottom of the same page**, linked to a **reference mark** (usually a superscript number¹) in the main text. It gives a **source, explanation or extra detail** without interrupting the main text.
Like a footnote, but all the notes are collected at the **end of the document** (or of a chapter) instead of at the bottom of each page.

blocks.caption: Footnotes and endnotes

items.title: What footnotes are used for in project documentation
items.content:
- **Citing sources** — the book, website or standard a fact comes from (avoids **plagiarism**).
- **Explaining a technical term** or abbreviation for a non-expert reader (e.g. "SQL — Structured Query Language").
- **Extra detail** that would break the flow of the main text (version numbers, exceptions, comments).
- **Cross-references** to another section, appendix or document.

items.title: Why use footnotes rather than brackets in the text
items.content:
- The main text stays **short and easy to read**.
- The note is on the **same page**, so the reader does not have to search for it.
- Numbering is **automatic** — notes are renumbered when text is added or moved.

blocks.title: Footnotes in a test report
blocks.content:
*All tests were run on the school's server¹ using the test data described in the test plan².*

---
¹ Windows Server 2022, 16 GB RAM, PostgreSQL 16.
² See Appendix B, Table 4.

blocks.title: Footnotes vs endnotes
rows: Quick — no need to turn pages
The reader must go to the end
Short explanations, sources the reader needs immediately
Long lists of references; documents with many notes

blocks.title: Inserting a footnote
items: Place the cursor where the reference mark should go.
**References → Insert Footnote** (Word) / **Insert → Footnote** (Google Docs); shortcut **Ctrl + Alt + F** in Word.
Type the note at the bottom of the page.
To convert footnotes to endnotes: **References → Footnotes → Convert**.

blocks.content:
- Using footnotes for **main** information — they are for sources and extra detail.
- Typing the number ¹ by hand — it will not renumber when notes are added.
- Writing a source as just "Google" or "internet" — give the **author / title / URL and date**.
An arrangement of information in **rows and columns** of **cells**, used to present related data so that it is **easy to read, compare and find**.
A **numbered title** above or below a table or figure ("Table 4. Test plan for the age field"), so that it can be **referred to in the text** and listed automatically.

rows: Field name, data type, size, key, validation, description
Test no., description, test data, type of data, expected result, actual result
Task, start date, end date, person responsible

| 1 | Valid age accepted | 15 | Normal | Accepted | Accepted ✔ |

items.title: Good practice for tables
items.content:
- A **header row** with clear column headings (bold, shaded); **repeat the header row** on each page if the table continues.
- A **caption** with a number and title so it can be referred to in the text.
- **Consistent** alignment: text left, numbers right or centred.
- Use **borders and shading** to make rows easy to follow; avoid too many colours.
- **Merge cells** for headings that span several columns; do not split a row across pages.
- Keep the table **simple** — one type of information per column.

items.title: Inserting and formatting a table
items.content:
- **Insert → Table**, choose the number of rows and columns.
- **Table Design / Layout** tabs: header row, banded rows, borders, merge and split cells, column width, alignment.
- **Repeat header rows** (Layout → Repeat Header Rows).
- **References → Insert Caption** to number the table automatically.
- **Insert → Table of Figures** creates a list of all tables in the document.

blocks.title: Why use a table instead of a paragraph?
rows: "Test 1 used 15, which is normal data; the expected result was accepted and it was accepted. Test 2 used 11, a boundary value…"
The same information in rows and columns — each value in its own cell, easy to **scan, compare and check**
Find a value by its **row and column**
Easy to miss a test or a result
**Empty cells** show at once what is missing

blocks.content:
- Tables without **column headings** or **captions**.
- Putting different kinds of data in the same column.
- A header row that does not repeat when the table runs onto the next page.

A list at the **start of a document** of its **headings** (chapters and sections) with the **page number** of each, used to **navigate** the document. In a word processor it is **generated automatically** from text formatted with **heading styles** and can be **updated** with one click.

blocks.caption: An automatic table of contents is built from heading styles

blocks.title: Creating an automatic table of contents
items: Format every chapter title with **Heading 1** and every section title with **Heading 2** (Home → Styles).
Place the cursor on an empty page after the title page.
**References → Table of Contents** (Word) / **Insert → Table of contents** (Google Docs) and choose a style.
After editing the document, click **Update Table** (update the entire table) so that headings and page numbers are correct.
Hold **Ctrl** and click an entry to jump to that section (hyperlinks).

blocks.title: Automatic vs typed table of contents
rows: Each line and page number typed
Every number must be checked and retyped
Wrong or missing page numbers are common

items.title: Why a project document needs a TOC
items.content:
- Readers (teacher, client, programmers) can **find a section quickly**.
- Shows the **structure** of the document at a glance — which parts are included.
- Works together with **page numbers in the footer**: the TOC gives the page, the footer shows where you are.

items.title: Related automatic lists
items.content:
- **Table of figures** — a list of all diagrams with their captions.
- **List of tables** — from table captions (Insert Table of Figures → label "Table").
- **Index** — key words with the pages where they appear.

blocks.title: Worked example — TOC for a project report
blocks.content:
Daniyar's report has chapters *1 Analysis*, *2 Design*, *3 Development*, *4 Testing*, *5 Evaluation*, each with sections such as *2.1 DFD* and *2.2 Data dictionary*.
1. He applies **Heading 1** to the chapter titles and **Heading 2** to the section titles.
2. On page 2 he inserts an automatic **table of contents**.
3. He adds three pages of screenshots to chapter 3, so chapters 4 and 5 move — he clicks **Update Table** and every page number in the TOC is corrected.
4. A heading he typed in bold but without a style is missing from the TOC — he applies **Heading 2** and updates again.

- Making headings **bold and large by hand** instead of using **heading styles** — they do not appear in the TOC.
- Forgetting to **update** the TOC after editing, so page numbers are wrong.
- Confusing the **table of contents** (headings + pages) with a **table** (rows and columns of data).

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: A fragment of a page of the "User guide 2025" is shown. Name the element at the top of the page that contains the text "User guide 2025 — page 3". [1]**
**Header** (1).

**Q: Give two items that need to be included in the user guide. [2]**
**Installation instructions** / the steps required to install the product (1); details of **backup procedures** / required **hardware and software** / how to use each function / **troubleshooting** (1).

**Q: Explain why the programmer should use a footer with page numbers in the technical documentation. [2]**
The page numbers appear **automatically on every page** (1), so readers can **find sections from the table of contents** and notice if pages are **missing** (1).

**Q: Explain one reason for using footnotes in a project report. [2]**
To **cite the source** of information (1) without interrupting the main text, so the report is easy to read and avoids **plagiarism** (1).

**Q: Explain why the test results should be presented in a table. [2]**
Each test's data, expected and actual result are in **separate columns** (1), so they are **easy to compare** and failed tests can be found quickly (1).

**Q: Describe how to create a table of contents that stays correct when the document changes. [3]**
Apply **heading styles** (Heading 1, Heading 2) to the chapter and section titles (1); insert an **automatic table of contents** (References → Table of Contents) (1); **update the table** after editing so the page numbers are correct (1).

- Typing page numbers or footnote numbers by hand instead of using **automatic fields**.
- Confusing a **header** with a **heading**, and a **footnote** with a **footer**.
- Using footnotes for **main** information — they are for sources and extra detail.
- Tables without **column headings** or **captions**.
- A table of contents that was not **updated** after the last edit.
